Lipoma: The patient presents with a firm, nonpulsatile mass in the left medial thigh that is fixed to underlying tissues but mobile relative to the overlying skin. The mass is described as having a density similar to subcutaneous fat on CT scan and appears as a fatty-appearing, well-circumscribed mass with internal septations on MRI. These imaging characteristics, combined with the lack of signs of inflammation, neurovascular impairment, or inguinal lymphadenopathy, are consistent with a benign lipomatous tumor, most likely a lipoma.
Atypical Lipomatous Tumor: Given the location and imaging characteristics of the mass, including its well-circumscribed nature and internal septations, an atypical lipomatous tumor (ALT) is also a consideration. ALTs are intermediate entities between benign lipomas and malignant liposarcomas and can exhibit varying degrees of cellular atypia and proliferative activity.
